analysis.one_liner: Sets the federal minimum wage so a full-time worker earns 15% above the poverty line.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to committee the day it was introduced and never received a House vote before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would replace the fixed federal minimum wage with a formula: the Labor Department would set the wage at whatever hourly rate lets a person working 40 hours a week, 52 weeks a year, earn 15% more than the federal poverty threshold for a family of four. The Department would set the first rate by June 2017 and update it every four years, and could never lower the rate once set. States and cities could still set higher minimums.
analysis.who_benefits: Full-time minimum wage workers, most of whom the bill's own findings note currently earn below the poverty threshold for a family of four. Their pay would rise to at least a modest cushion above that line, and re-set every four years so it does not erode with inflation between acts of Congress.

how_it_helps.text: A full-time worker earning the federal minimum wage earns an income below the federal poverty threshold for a family of four (two adults, two children), according to the bill's findings.

The bill requires the Labor Department to set the minimum wage at the hourly rate that yields an annual income 15% above the poverty threshold for a family of four, based on 40 hours a week for 52 weeks.
The Department would review the rate every four years and publish it in the Federal Register, so the wage would adjust over time rather than waiting for Congress to act.
The Secretary is barred from adjusting the minimum wage to a lower rate than the one in effect.
States, territories, tribes, and local governments remain free to set a higher minimum wage than the federal floor.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that pay the federal minimum wage — restaurants, retailers, and other low-wage employers — would bear higher payroll costs, and some would pass costs to consumers through prices or reduce hours. The bill's findings also point to housing costs: it cites data showing one-bedroom rent averages more than 65% of a full-time minimum wage worker's income, and that even two full-time minimum wage earners fall below the income needed to afford an average one-bedroom apartment.

drawbacks.text: The bill sets a single national rate based on the poverty threshold for the 48 contiguous states, with no adjustment for the very different living costs in Alaska, Hawaii, or high-cost cities.
The wage would be set by the Labor Department rather than by Congress directly, moving the setting of a major wage floor into an executive-branch formula.

Because the first rate would take effect with no phase-in schedule in the bill, low-margin employers relying on minimum wage labor would face a sudden payroll increase, and some economists warn large abrupt increases can reduce entry-level hiring — a cost an honest supporter would have to weigh against the raise for workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers covered, the gain is substantial: the bill's own findings show full-time minimum wage pay falls below the family poverty line, and the formula would lift it above that line permanently. The costs fall on employers and partly on consumers through prices, and the one-size national formula fits high- and low-cost regions imperfectly. On balance this is a large, targeted transfer of income to the lowest-paid workers, with real but conventional economic tradeoffs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee on January 3, 2017, and no markup, hearing, or vote ever followed before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Al Green introduced the bill in the House on January 3, 2017, the first day of the 115th Congress.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day.
No further action was taken — no committee markup, no floor vote, no Senate action — for the remainder of the Congress.
The 115th Congress ended in January 2019, and the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay the federal minimum wage are better off, because the wage floor they pay never rose; the roughly 43 million Americans in poverty cited in the bill's findings gained nothing from the bill's failure.

for.name: Rep. Al Green
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Original Living Wage Act of 2017 on the first day of the 115th Congress.

for.name: 10 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, all from the Democratic Party.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-NC)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 3, 2017 and never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled committee took no action; no vote was ever recorded, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.industry: Low-wage employers (restaurants, retail, hospitality, and other minimum wage industries)
industries.note: The bill would have raised the pay floor for their workers to at least 15% above the family poverty line, increasing payroll costs. The industry's interest in keeping the current floor runs directly against the wage gain for workers.

industries.industry: Minimum wage workers and their households
industries.note: Their wages would rise and then ratchet up every four years, with no downward adjustment permitted. This is the group the bill is built around.
